1:
Calvin sets the frame. Many imagined that under Christ’s reign the Church would enjoy tranquillity, the prophets having promised real peace at his coming; the apostle answers that its condition under the gospel will be no different from what it was under the law, and no particular time is named, so all ages are included. He adds the point of the comparison: the trial of our faith is like the fathers’, and for the same reason, that it may be made evident whether we really love God. Henry says the same more briefly: when God sends true prophets, the devil sends some to seduce.

Who the men were is less clear than they would like. Barnes and Clarke reach for the same list — Ebionites, Cerinthians, Nicolaitans, and the sects gathered under the name Gnostic — but Clarke enters a caution the others do not: of their opinions it is hard to form any satisfactory view, they were no doubt bad enough, and their opponents have doubtless made them worse. Ellicott notes the word for false teachers occurs here alone, probably formed on the analogy of false witnesses: men who teach what is false rather than men pretending to a teaching office.

On the word rendered heresies the philology is unanimous and the English is condemned. Robertson says it is simply a choosing, a school, a sect, used of Sadducees, Pharisees, and of Christians by Paul himself. Ellicott holds that neither sect nor heresy renders it, since in the New Testament it points to divisions rather than doctrines and always to parties inside the Church, not to bodies separated from it; he traces damnable heresies to the Geneva version and calls it altogether a change for the worse, preferring the older sects of perdition. Clarke agrees destructive would be better than damnable, and Wesley glosses heresies as divisions. Ellicott adds a count: the one Greek word for destruction stands six times in this short letter and is rendered five different ways.

Then comes the flashpoint. Ellicott declares the clause conclusive against Calvinistic doctrines of partial redemption, since the apostle says these impious teachers were bought; Wesley presses the same point in a sentence, that these very men perish everlastingly and therefore Christ bought even them that perish; Clarke, less sure whether the Father or the Son is meant, concludes for the Son and draws the same inference. Calvin does not meet the argument on that ground at all. He reads the denial as practical rather than doctrinal — Christ redeemed a people separated from the world’s pollutions, so those who throw off the bridle and give themselves to licentiousness are not unjustly said to deny the Christ who redeemed them. Gill, whose note breaks off mid-sentence before the clause, offers nothing. Two notice who is writing: Ellicott observes that the phrase is remarkable from one who himself denied his Master and asks whether a forger would have ventured it; Robertson remarks that denying was the very thing Peter did, even after Christ’s warning.

The second verse turns on a variant, and here they converge. Barnes cites three editors, Clarke some sixty manuscripts with the versions and several Greek fathers, Calvin that very few copies read perdition, and Ellicott says the received reading is undoubtedly wrong; all prefer lascivious or wanton ways, and Robertson prints it so without argument. On what follows they split. Barnes calls it a very remarkable circumstance that those who deny the essential doctrines have so frequently been licentious, corrupt men seeking the sanction of religion for their corruptions. Ellicott grants the connection was often real, and still is, but warns it was as often asserted without foundation, impurity being the standing charge against anyone of a different creed, between Christian and heathen and between Christians alike. Calvin measures the defection: hardly one in ten who once professed Christ keeps the purity of faith to the end.
3:
Covetousness draws the sharpest sociology here. Barnes observes that the religious principle is the strongest implanted in man, so men who can earn a living no other way turn public teachers and adopt whatever doctrine gives them most power over other men’s purses — true religion does ask its friends to devote all they have, and that requirement is easy to pervert. Ellicott corrects the preposition to in covetousness, the atmosphere these men live in, and sets them beside the Greek sophists who taught for money; he adds that a bombastic mysticism promising secrets of the unseen world was a lucrative profession in the last days of paganism, and passed into Christianity as an element in various heresies. Robertson puts it shortest: a merely intellectual Gnosticism bore fruit in immorality and fraud. Gill notes the coveting may be of applause as much as of money.

On the feigned words Clarke and Calvin arrive from opposite sides at one target. Calvin allows the Greek to mean either words not conveying real sentiments or invented tales, and the apparatus printed with him proposes fables of angelic visions and miracles at the tombs of saints, fabricated to draw money from the people. Clarke, quoting another writer, finds in the clause a prediction of the Romish clergy, who rated every crime at a fixed price, so that whoever pays may sin freely. Robertson renders it forged words, from a verb meaning to mould as from clay.

That the sentence has not lapsed is pressed by all. Ellicott and Robertson both note the verb means literally is not idle, and Ellicott adds the destruction is awake and on its way; Robertson observes that the word for slumbering appears elsewhere only of the virgins who slept, and that destruction has stood three times in as many verses. Barnes pictures justice as long attentive to their movements and impatient to do its work; Henry warns against assuming a reprieve is the forerunner of a pardon.

The first example divides them twice. On the construction, Ellicott says the sentence has no proper conclusion, the writer in his eagerness having lost the thread; Calvin denies any clause is missing, the answering statement standing in the ninth verse. On the sin, Barnes and Clarke refuse to guess — Clarke noting that the tradition of a fall of angels is in all countries and religions, but the accounts various and contradictory because there is no revelation on the point, so that conjecture is useless. Gill reports the common opinion, pride. Ellicott rejects the primeval fall outright: the Old Testament has no record of it and it affords no analogy to these teachers. He reads it instead of the angels of Genesis six as expounded in the Book of Enoch, and suggests the false teachers used that book, so the argument is aimed at them from their own authority. Robertson supplies unwitting support: Tartarus is where Enoch puts the fallen angels, Gehenna being kept for apostate Jews. Wesley notes the chains do not hinder them walking up and down seeking whom they may devour.

Clarke observes that the verb for casting down appears nowhere else in the New Testament nor in the Greek Old Testament, so its sense must come from the Greek poets; Robertson reports the manuscripts divided between chains and pits, preferring pits. Then Noah the eighth. Clarke defends the idiom from two Greek authors; Ellicott says the point is that only eight escaped out of a whole world, and dismisses both the mystical reading of the number and the notion that eighth means eighth from Enos; Robertson judges that taking eighth with preacher is hardly correct. Calvin, reporting the same dispute, is more interested in why Noah is called a preacher of righteousness: he laboured to restore a degenerate world not only by teaching but by the anxious toil of building the ark a hundred and twenty years.
6:
The third example is dispatched briefly. Barnes and Robertson both note the verb for turning to ashes occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, Robertson adding that a Roman historian used it of an eruption of Vesuvius. Ellicott points out that the word rendered overthrow is the very word the Greek Old Testament uses of these cities; Robertson reports that two modern editors reject it here on manuscript grounds. Clarke distinguishes three Greek words for example — a thing to be shunned, a thing to be followed, a bare exhibition — then admits the distinctions are not always observed. Calvin makes the larger claim: so memorable a stroke that when Scripture speaks of the destruction of the ungodly it alludes to it as the type, as the redemption from Egypt stands for the perpetual safety of the Church.

Calling Lot righteous is the difficulty, and two of them face it. Gill sets down what the Jewish writers say of him — a perfect wicked man, as wicked as the Sodomites, who chose to dwell among them because they abounded in sin — and gives the contrary verdict himself, that Lot was justified by an imputed righteousness. Ellicott grants the epithet looks at variance with a man who stayed in such a place for worldly advantage, and answers that righteous is relative, measured against the morality of the age and the licentiousness of his neighbours. He assembles the defence: the hospitality that Hebrews seems to hold up as a model, the rescue set beside the declaration that ten righteous men would have saved the city, the obedience when told to leave everything, and Zoar spared at his intercession. Henry and Barnes reach the same verdict by a rule: God does not account men just or unjust from one act, but from the general course of life.

How the eighth verse is construed divides them three ways. Barnes reports the Latin rendering, that in seeing and hearing he was just, followed by many expositors, but prefers the English. Calvin knows that as the common explanation, Lot being just in his eyes and ears because all his senses abhorred the crimes of Sodom, and prefers the other, that he tormented his soul by seeing and hearing. Robertson takes both nouns as instruments, and notes the verb for vexing stands in a tense of continued action, a word properly used of testing metals and then of torment. Clarke observes that the two Greek verbs are equally emphatic, and adds the arithmetic: Lot had lived at Sodom about twenty years.

What they draw from it is the same. Henry observes that being accustomed to wickedness did not reconcile Lot to it nor abate his horror, and that in bad company we escape neither guilt nor grief. Barnes says those who live among the wicked must see and hear much that pains them, and it is well if they do not grow indifferent. Calvin presses further: the sorrow was voluntary, and the godly who groan at the world rushing into evil have the more reason to groan for their own sins — said expressly lest, when impiety prevails, we be captivated by the allurements of vice and perish with the rest.

Ellicott turns the threefold repetition of righteous into an argument. Such repetitions, stigmatised as poverty of language, are natural in a man writing under strong emotion, who does not stop to pick his words, and more so in one writing a foreign language; they are not the laboured effort of a writer personating him, and that they abound here and not in the first epistle is a mark of genuineness. He adds that the bright side, deliverance set beside destruction, is wanting in the parallel epistle, and asks whether it is fanciful to see there the hand of one who had himself denied the Master that bought him and had yet been rescued like Lot.
9:
The long sentence begun six verses back finishes here, and the earlier quarrel about it settles. Robertson calls this the actual apodosis of the protasis begun at the angels, which is where Calvin had placed it; Ellicott concedes the main clause but still finds the construction disjointed through the writer’s eagerness, the clause itself interrupted by the words about delivering the godly when what he chiefly wanted to prove was the reserving of the ungodly.

A tense is then corrected, and the correction carries doctrine. Ellicott says the participle is present, not future: not to be punished but being punished, so that these are already under punishment while they wait for the final doom — and he calls the error the same that turned a phrase in Acts into such as should be saved instead of those who were being saved. Robertson reaches the same conclusion, the present tense emphasising the continuity of the punishment; Barnes reads it out of the case of the angels, who seem to go at large yet are kept under control for their trial.

On the deliverance the four are complementary. Clarke reduces it to a rule in three parts: the godly man is not preserved from temptation, he is preserved in it, and he is delivered out of it. Barnes lists the means — an angel to take the tempted by the hand, the tempter’s power broken, friends raised up, or removal to heaven — and adds that God often sees a way we should not have thought of. Calvin puts the offence the verse is meant to remove as an objection: if the Lord would have his own safe, why does he not gather them into some corner of the earth to stimulate one another to holiness, instead of mingling them with the wicked? Gill takes the temptations to be not Satan’s solicitations but afflictions, so called because they try faith and patience; Wesley says only that the instances prove God has the wisdom, the power and the will.

Then the sharpest division in the chapter. What are the dignities that these men rail at? Calvin says there is no doubt the words refer to imperial and magisterial power, since the magistrate’s office excels every other; Barnes takes them as men of exalted rank and reads the clause politically, as the mark of advocates for unbridled freedom, declaimers on liberty and oppression who secretly lust for the very power they would deny others; Clarke has them blaspheming civil government and wishing all government destroyed that they might live as they list; Wesley glosses them flatly as persons in authority. Ellicott denies it: the exact meaning is not clear, but the context shows that spiritual powers alone are intended and that earthly powers, civil or ecclesiastical, are not included, much less exclusively meant — these men deny the existence of the spiritual agencies by which God governs the world, or speak slightingly of them. Robertson inclines the same way, suggesting the dignities are angels.

Two smaller notes belong here. Ellicott calls the English version minutely perverse in this verse, since it renders one Greek word two ways and two Greek words one way between this passage and its parallel, and he holds that a fresh verse should begin at the word presumptuous, the construction being entirely changed and the subject returning from sensual persons at large to the false teachers in particular. On the walking after the flesh, Gill takes it of strange flesh rather than of corrupt nature generally, and Clarke of practices he names plainly, while Ellicott notes the phrase is less definite here than in the parallel and applies to sensual persons at large. Calvin makes it the mark of men given up like brute animals to the desire of the flesh, and Henry the rule that evil opinions are commonly accompanied by evil practices.
11:
Whom the angels decline to rail at follows the previous division. Barnes and Clarke both send the reader to the tradition of the archangel disputing over the body of Moses, Clarke adding Zechariah’s vision and the remark that the archangel treated a damned spirit courteously, saying only, the Lord rebuke thee. Robertson takes the ones not railed at to be the evil angels. Calvin will have none of it: the angels are the holy ones and the objects the magistrates, and the reading that makes them devils fails because Satan, the author of every blasphemy, could never be so moderate as to spare men. He grounds it historically — every magistrate of that day was an ungodly and bloody enemy of the gospel, hateful to the angels who guard the Church, and yet they did not condemn them, out of respect to a power divinely appointed. Gill agrees, making the angels greater not than devils but than kings and magistrates.

Ellicott uses these two verses to argue which epistle came first. He concedes that the eleventh, intelligible only beside the parallel, looks at first like an abridgement of it, and answers three ways: the allusion may have been to a tradition well enough known to need no explaining; the contest meant may be Zechariah’s rather than the one over Moses; or no contest may be meant at all, only angels declining to denounce these men and leaving them to God’s judgment. He adds that if the abridgement is granted the argument turns round, since a writer with the other text before him would hardly deface it so. At the twelfth he presses the reverse: the parallel is so much better made, its antithesis between abusing what men cannot know and misusing what they cannot help knowing so telling, that improvement is likelier than spoiling.

On the beasts the best remark is Ellicott’s. He would take the word rendered natural as an adverb rather than an epithet: these animals cannot help themselves, it is their nature to rush after what will prove their ruin, whereas the false teachers seek their own destruction voluntarily and against nature. Robertson renders it born mere animals for capture and destruction; Calvin says they are induced by no allurements but of themselves hasten into the snares of Satan. Barnes draws the moral, that a man who sinks to the level of brutes must expect to be treated like one; Clarke has them taken with nets and gins, first imprisoned and then judged. Wesley alone reserves that such creatures seem born to be taken and destroyed only in the present disordered state of the world.

Rioting in the daytime is read one way by three and another by Ellicott. Clarke says most sinners seek the secrecy of night, but these bid defiance to decency and proclaim their impurities to the sun; Wesley has them glorying to do it in the face of the sun; Barnes says only the shameless revel in open day. Ellicott objects that riot is too strong, the word meaning dainty living, and that dainty fare in the daytime has no point; he proposes instead for the day, without thought for the morrow, counting the luxury of the moment a pleasure — the doctrine of the Cyrenaics and the instinct of the beasts just mentioned.

The verse closes on another variant. Barnes reports that several versions and a few manuscripts read love-feasts for deceivings, and judges the common reading correct; Clarke judges the opposite, and infers that these men held a kind of communion with the Church and desecrated its sacred festivals; Robertson sets the manuscripts against each other without deciding; Calvin keeps both, rioting in their own delusions and feasting together with you. Ellicott, hedging on the reading, notes instead that spots and blemishes answer exactly to the words used in the first epistle of the lamb without blemish and without spot.
14:
The eyes come first. Gill notes that the Jewish teachers held the seventh commandment broken by an unchaste look, and Barnes builds on that: the eye is usually the first offender and the inlet to the desire, and there is much in dress and gesture fitted to deepen it. Robertson has the picture of a man who cannot see a woman without lascivious thought. Ellicott presses the grammar — they cannot be made to cease from sin — and finds the reason in their principle: because they refused to suffer in the flesh and gave it licence deliberately, they could not stop. Clarke reports a variant yielding eyes full of adultery and incessant sin, the images floating continually before a disordered fancy.

Two metaphors follow. Ellicott renders the next word enticing with bait, notes the fishing figure occurs twice in this letter and once elsewhere in the New Testament, and remarks that it may point to a fisherman of Galilee. Calvin uses the same figure, comparing their arts to hooks that catch the unwary, and adds that those who let themselves be lured have no excuse, the fault being their own levity where faith has struck no root. On the heart exercised, Clarke and Robertson both hear the gymnasium, the word being that used of men training for the public games. Calvin prefers lusts to covetousness, inward vices being meant after the outward; and on the last phrase offers a choice, that these were children of cursing either actively, bringing a curse wherever they went, or passively, deserving one. Ellicott takes it the second way, malediction having adopted them as its own.

One misspelt name draws four separate explanations. Barnes offers three at once — a corrupted text, a father with two names, or a change made for Greek ease of pronunciation — and notes the Greek Old Testament has the ordinary form. Clarke traces it to the confusion of two Hebrew letters that closely resemble each other. Wesley says simply that the Chaldeans pronounced it so. Ellicott agrees it is a dialectal variation arising from Aramaic pronunciation, and turns it to his running argument, calling it a slight indication that the writer was a Palestinian Jew.

Barnes draws the likeness to Balaam furthest, listing three points — that he was a professed servant of God, that he was covetous, and that he led others into the very sin these men did, having counselled the Moabites to entice Israel by their women. Ellicott adds that a comparison with the letters to the seven churches gives countenance to including the Nicolaitans, and that the past tenses here suit the view that the chapter is genuine prediction, a future foretold with such confidence being commonly spoken of as already past. Calvin asks by what right Balaam bore the name of prophet at all, being addicted to many superstitions, and answers that the gift was special, and that God has sometimes caused prophecy to exist in the midst of idolatry so that men might have less excuse.

The ass closes the passage and settles an old objection. Ellicott corrects forbad to hindered, and the supposed discrepancy with the history disappears: it was not the angel but the ass that hindered Balaam’s infatuation from hurrying him to destruction. He adds that the word for madness is a rare formation, perhaps coined here, probably chosen for its sound beside the word for prophet; Robertson confirms it is the only known instance of the form. Clarke produces the striking parallel: in two of the Targums the ass says, Woe to thee, Balaam, thou sinner, thou madman, there is no wisdom found in thee. Calvin dwells on the indignity: the angel made himself known to the ass before the prophet, and the mouth of the beast was opened so that a man unwilling to submit to God might have her for his teacher.
17:
The two figures are read alike by everyone. Barnes puts the traveller in the hot sand coming to a dry well, and adds that a rising cloud raises the farmer’s hope before the wind carries it off. Clarke has the same and sharpens it: these men are sowers with no seed in their basket. Gill says they looked like angels of light and held nothing but the filth of a dry well. Calvin makes the point of both figures that the appearance was fallacious, and turns the second into the sentence: for the momentary darkness they spread, a thicker darkness is prepared for ever. Wesley needs one line — fountains and clouds promise water, and so do these, but do not perform — and Henry adds that as clouds hinder the sun, so these darken counsel by words without truth. Clarke and Robertson prefer the reading mists to clouds.

Ellicott stops to weigh an argument about the original language. One Hebrew word occurring twice in the Old Testament is rendered by the Septuagint in one place by the word used here for well and in the other by the word the parallel epistle uses for cloud; so the same Hebrew might have produced wells without water in one letter and clouds without water in the other, which has been urged in favour of a Hebrew original for both. He will not have it on those terms: such coincidences may easily be accidents of language, and must be shown to be numerous before a solid argument can rest on them, especially as both writers were Jews writing Greek while thinking in Hebrew, so that one thought might take two Greek forms.

On the swelling words Barnes writes the chapter’s best sentence: truth is simple and delights in simple statements, expecting to make its way by its own force, while error is noisy and declamatory and hopes to succeed by substituting sound for sense. Ellicott sums it as exaggeration, unreality, boastfulness and emptiness — great pretensions and no results, carrying on the figure of the dry wells. Calvin names a second-century teacher who coined words unheard of before, by whose empty sound the unlearned were ensnared, and finds fanatics of the same kind in his own day. Clarke thinks of the Nicolaitans.

Ellicott then corrects both verb and adverb in the next clause, and the sense turns over. The received text has those that were clean escaped; the true reading is those who are scarcely escaping, the participle present and not past, the persons meant being the unstable souls mentioned earlier. He accounts for the corruption elegantly: an unfamiliar Greek word was turned by a slight alteration into a familiar one much like it. Robertson gives the manuscripts on each side and prefers the same. The victims are therefore not converts who had got clear away and were dragged back, but people barely getting out.

The promised liberty draws the last disagreement. Ellicott points to what one heresiarch is reported by two fathers to have taught as a specimen of the freedom meant: freed from righteousness to become slaves of sin. Barnes says true religion always produces liberty, and what these men offered was freedom from what they took for needless restraint. Clarke explains the closing maxim from the Roman law of war, by which the conquered might be killed or kept as slaves. Calvin enters a caution the rest do not: it does not follow that a wicked man cannot preach usefully of Christ’s benefits, for what is condemned is vicious doctrine joined to impurity of life; and he defines the true liberty as exemption from the curse of the law in order to deliverance from the dominion of sin, so that where lusts reign the liberty of Christ has no place at all. Ellicott hears an echo of a saying of the Lord which this writer may himself have heard.
20:
Clarke takes the word for pollutions literally. It was used of the noxious effluvia from bodies infected with disease, from corpses and stagnant marshes, so that the world is one putrid marsh sending off its vapours in every direction; and he improves the image with a saying of a Latin father, that the whole world is one great diseased man stretched from east to west, to heal whom the almighty Physician came down from heaven. Gill notes the phrase is rabbinical. Ellicott corrects the preposition again: they escaped in knowledge, not through it, the knowledge being that in which the escape consists.

Whether these men had ever been Christians is the question here. Barnes denies it twice over: escaping the pollutions of the world need not mean they were true Christians, since men may reform outwardly with no grace at heart, and knowing the doctrines well enough to abandon vicious habits is not saving knowledge. Ellicott says the opposite from the same words — the knowledge named is the mature and complete kind spoken of in the first chapter, which shows these men were well-instructed Christians. Calvin, without arguing the point, calls them men consecrated to God led back to their old filth, who wilfully extinguished the light and, so far as they could, profaned the covenant ratified by the blood of Christ. Robertson observes only that it is unclear whether the subject is the victims or the teachers, and names a scholar on each side.

That it were better not to have known is agreed. Barnes gives three reasons — they would not have dishonoured religion, nor sunk so deep, nor incurred so heavy a condemnation — and adds that if men are resolved to be wicked they had better never pretend to be good. Calvin puts it as a rule of service, that the servant who knowingly despises his lord’s commands deserves a twofold punishment. Ellicott turns it into an epigram, that to have loved a great truth and lost it is what often wrecks a life.

The two proverbs are examined closely. Ellicott notes that if the first comes from Proverbs we have an independent rendering of the Hebrew, the Greek version translating it quite otherwise with dog the only word in common; that the second is not in the Old Testament at all; and that both may come from popular tradition rather than Scripture. He adds that the word for vomit may have been coined by the writer. Robertson thinks the second saying Gentile in origin, being about hogs, and cites a heathen moralist and a story of a hog that bathed with people of quality and then found a stinking drain. Clarke adds a rabbinic parallel about Orphah returning to her mire and a Greek one advising a man to reason with the swine.

Then the sharpest exchange in the chapter. Barnes holds the proverbs decisive: the dog and the swine had never been anything but dog and swine, so these persons had never been anything but sinners, there had been no real change of heart and therefore no falling away, and the passage should not be quoted to prove that true Christians may fall from grace and perish. Clarke reads the same verse as a sad proof of the possibility of falling from grace, and from high degrees of it, since these had truly repented and been washed from all their filthiness, which must have been through the blood of the Lamb. Calvin takes a third road: the fault is wholly their own because they are pigs and dogs, so no part of the sin can be ascribed to the gospel — which is a medicine that purges by wholesome vomiting, and a laver that cleanses, though many swine roll in the mud again as soon as they are washed. Wesley says only that such are all men before grace and after shipwreck.
